claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by the stability and evolution of nanoscale oxide dispersoids at grain boundaries.
High-temperature toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by the stability and evolution of nanoscale oxide dispersoids at grain boundaries.
Stable oxide dispersoids inhibit grain-boundary sliding.
Dislocation and grain-boundary pinning by stable dispersoids reduces high-temperature plastic strain rate.
Stable oxide dispersoids improve toughness at elevated temperatures.
Coarsening or dissolution of oxide dispersoids makes dislocation motion less constrained.
Coarsening or dissolution of oxide dispersoids makes grain-boundary sliding or migration less constrained.
Controlled thermal annealing can induce oxide-dispersoid coarsening or partial dissolution.
A coarsened-dispersoid condition will have a higher high-temperature plastic strain rate than the untreated stable-dispersoid baseline.
A coarsened-dispersoid condition will have lower toughness than the untreated stable-dispersoid baseline.
A coarsened-dispersoid condition will have lower yield strength than the untreated stable-dispersoid baseline.
A coarsened-dispersoid condition will show an earlier onset of plastic deformation under cyclic or sustained loading.
Temperatures of approximately 600–1000 °C are representative of conditions encountered by fusion plasma-facing components.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to alloys engineered with nanoscale oxide dispersoids and microstructures similar to current fusion-relevant alloys.
The dispersoid-mediated effect may differ when diffusion-controlled creep or another deformation mechanism dominates.
